units.ti: Preferences as consistent answers to a questionnaire
units.g: Rubinstein’s primary definition: preferences are a function answering every pairwise comparison, free of order effects and transitive.
units.s: Preferences on a set X are a function f that assigns to every pair (x,y) of distinct elements of X one of three answers, x ≻ y, y ≻ x or I (indifference), such that: No order effect: f(x,y) = f(y,x) for all distinct x, y ∈ X. Transitivity: for all pairwise distinct x, y, z ∈ X, if f(x,y) = x ≻ y and f(y,z) = y ≻ z then f(x,z) = x ≻ z; and if f(x,y) = I and f(y,z) = I then f(x,z) = I. Here x ≻ y and I are labels for…

units.g: From the questionnaire definition: x ≻ y and y ∼ z imply x ≻ z.
units.s: Let f be preferences on X in the sense of Definition 1, and let x, y, z ∈ X be pairwise distinct. If f(x,y) = x ≻ y and f(y,z) = I, then f(x,z) = x ≻ z.
units.kw: PI-transitivity · mixed transitivity · Preferences · Did we require too little?

units.g: From the questionnaire definition: x ∼ y and y ≻ z imply x ≻ z.
units.s: Let f be preferences on X in the sense of Definition 1, and let x, y, z ∈ X be pairwise distinct. If f(x,y) = I and f(y,z) = y ≻ z, then f(x,z) = x ≻ z.

units.g: The standard definition: a reflexive, complete and transitive binary relation “at least as good as”.
units.s: A binary relation ≿ on a set X, read “x ≿ y: x is at least as preferred as y”, is a preference relation if it is reflexive: x ≿ x for every x ∈ X; complete: for all distinct x, y ∈ X, x ≿ y or y ≿ x; transitive: for all x, y, z ∈ X, if x ≿ y and y ≿ z, then x ≿ z.
units.kw: preference relation · completeness · transitivity · Preference relation · Completeness · Reflexivity · Transitivity · Preferences

units.ti: Equivalence of the two definitions of preferences
units.g: Questionnaire preferences and preference relations are in one-to-one correspondence, with matching meanings of strict preference and indifference.
units.s: For preferences f on X in the sense of Definition 1, let Translation(f) be the relation defined by x ≿ x for every x and, for distinct x, y, x ≿ y if and only if f(x,y) ∈ x ≻ y, I. Then: Translation(f) is a preference relation (Definition 2); it is one-to-one: if Translation(f₁) = Translation(f₂), then f₁(x,y) = f₂(x,y) for all distinct x, y; it is onto: every preference relation equals Translation(f) for some f; it…

units.g: A utility function represents a preference relation when one alternative is at least as good as another exactly when its utility is at least as high.
units.s: Let ≿ be a preference relation on X. A function U : X → ℝ represents ≿ if for all x, y ∈ X, x ≿ y ⟺ U(x) ≥ U(y). Such a U is a utility function for ≿, and ≿ has a utility representation if some U represents it.
units.kw: utility function · utility representation · Utility representation · Continuous utility representation · Integer-valued utility representation · Utility · The Concept of Utility Representation

units.ti: Utility is ordinal: strictly increasing transformations
units.g: Composing a utility function with any strictly increasing function gives another representation of the same preference.
units.s: Let ≿ be a preference relation on X, let U : X → ℝ represent ≿, and let f : ℝ → ℝ be strictly increasing. Then V = f ∘ U also represents ≿.
units.kw: ordinal utility · monotone transformation · Utility is ordinal · Ordinal utility · Utility · The Concept of Utility Representation

units.ti: Best and worst elements of finite sets
units.g: Every nonempty finite set has a best and a worst element under a preference relation.
units.s: Let ≿ be a preference relation on X and let A ⊆ X be finite and nonempty. Then A has a minimal element under ≿, some a ∈ A with x ≿ a for all x ∈ A, and a maximal element under ≿, some b ∈ A with b ≿ x for all x ∈ A.
units.kw: maximal element · minimal element · Best element of a set (maximal for the preference) · Utility · Existence of a Utility Representation

units.g: Every preference relation on a finite set has a utility representation with natural-number values.
units.s: Let X be finite and let ≿ be a preference relation on X. Then there is N : X → ℕ such that for all x, y ∈ X, x ≿ y ⟺ N(x) ≥ N(y).
units.kw: utility representation · finite set · Utility · Existence of a Utility Representation

units.g: Every preference relation on a countable set has a utility representation with values in (0, 1).
units.s: Let X be countable (finite or countably infinite) and let ≿ be a preference relation on X. Then there is U : X → ℝ that represents ≿ and satisfies 0 < U(x) < 1 for every x ∈ X.
units.kw: utility representation · countable set · Utility on countable sets · Countable utility representation · Utility · Existence of a Utility Representation

units.g: A list of preferences, consulted in order of priority, induces a lexicographic preference.
units.s: Let ≿₁, …, ≿_K be preference relations on X. The lexicographic preference ≿_L they induce is defined by x ≿L y if either there is k such that x ∼ₖ y for all k < k* and x ≻ₖ* y, or x ∼ₖ y for all k.
units.kw: lexicographic preference · Lexicographic preference · Lexicographic preferences · Utility · Lexicographic Preferences

units.ti: The lexicographic preference on the unit square
units.g: The standard example: on [0, 1]², the first coordinate decides and the second breaks ties.
units.s: On the unit square X = [0,1] × [0,1], the lexicographic preference induced by the two coordinate orders (x ≿ₖ y iff xₖ ≥ yₖ, for k = 1, 2) is aligned & (a₁, a₂) ≿_L (b₁, b₂) ⟺ \ & a₁ > b₁, or \ & a₁ = b₁ and a₂ ≥ b₂. aligned
units.kw: lexicographic preference · Lexicographic preference · lexicographic order (unit square) · The lexicographic order on the square is a preference relation · Utility · Lexicographic Preferences

units.g: The lexicographic preference induced by finitely many preference relations is complete and transitive.
units.s: Let ≿₁, …, ≿_K be preference relations on X. The lexicographic preference ≿_L they induce is a preference relation on X.
units.kw: lexicographic preference · Utility · Lexicographic Preferences

units.ti: No utility representation for the lexicographic preference on the unit square
units.g: The lexicographic preference on the unit square is complete and transitive, yet no real-valued function represents it.
units.s: Let ≿_L be the lexicographic preference on [0,1]²: (a₁,a₂) ≿_L (b₁,b₂) if a₁ > b₁, or a₁ = b₁ and a₂ ≥ b₂. There is no function u : [0,1]² → ℝ such that x ≿_L y ⟺ u(x) ≥ u(y) for all x, y.
units.kw: lexicographic preference · non-representability · The lexicographic counterexample · Lexicographic preference has no utility representation · Utility · Lexicographic Preferences

units.g: Strict preference is preserved under small perturbations of both alternatives.
units.s: Let X be a metric space (for example a subset of ℝⁿ) and ≿ a preference relation on X. Then ≿ is continuous if whenever a ≻ b (that is, not b ≿ a) there are balls B_a around a and B_b around b such that x ≻ y for all x ∈ B_a and y ∈ B_b.
units.kw: continuous preferences · Continuity of preferences (C1, open balls) · continuous preference relation · Continuity of preferences · Utility · Continuity of Preferences

units.g: The graph of a continuous preference relation is a closed set.
units.s: Let X be a metric space and ≿ a preference relation on X. Then ≿ is continuous if its graph (x,y) ∈ X × X : x ≿ y is a closed subset of X × X; equivalently, whenever aₙ ≿ bₙ for all n, aₙ → a and bₙ → b, also a ≿ b.
units.kw: continuous preferences · closed graph · Continuity of preferences (C2, closed graph) · continuous preference relation (closed graph) · Utility · Continuity of Preferences

units.ti: Equivalence of the two definitions of continuity
units.g: On a metric space, the open-ball and closed-graph definitions of continuous preferences agree.
units.s: Let X be a metric space and ≿ a preference relation on X. Then ≿ is continuous in the open-ball sense if and only if its graph (x,y) : x ≿ y is closed in X × X.
units.kw: continuous preferences · Utility · Continuity of Preferences

units.g: A continuous preference relation on a convex, or more generally connected, subset of Euclidean space has a continuous utility function.
units.s: Let X ⊆ ℝⁿ be convex and let ≿ be a continuous preference relation on X. Then there is a continuous function U : X → ℝ that represents ≿.
units.kw: Debreu’s theorem · continuous utility · utility representation · Continuous utility representation · Debreu’s theorem on a connected domain · Debreu’s representation theorem · Utility · Debreu's Theorem

units.g: Choices are observed on a domain of nonempty menus drawn from a grand set of alternatives.
units.s: A choice problem is a nonempty subset of a grand set X. A context (X, D) consists of X and a set D of subsets of X, each of which is a choice problem; D is the domain on which the agent’s behavior is defined.
units.kw: choice problem · Context (grand set and domain of choice problems) · Choice · Choice Functions

units.g: A choice function selects one alternative from every menu in its domain.
units.s: Given a context (X, D), a choice function C assigns to every A ∈ D an element C(A) ∈ A.
units.kw: choice function · Choice function · Choice · Choice Functions

units.g: The choice function that picks the best element of each menu according to a fixed preference.
units.s: Let (X, D) be a context and ≿ a preference relation on X, and assume that every A ∈ D has a unique best element under ≿, an a ∈ A with a ≿ x for all x ∈ A. The induced (rational) choice function C_≿ assigns to each A ∈ D its best element under ≿.
units.kw: rational choice · induced choice function · Choice function induced by a preference (rational choice) · Best element of a set (maximal for the preference) · rational choice function · Choice · Rational Choice Functions

units.g: A choice function is rationalizable if it coincides with the rational choice function of some preference relation.
units.s: A choice function C for a context (X, D) can be rationalized if there is a preference relation ≿ on X such that every A ∈ D has a unique best element under ≿ and C(A) = C_≿(A) for every A ∈ D.
units.kw: rationalizability · Rationalizable choice function · rationalizable choice function · Rationalizable choice · Choice · Rationalizing

units.g: Contraction consistency: an alternative chosen from a menu is still chosen from any smaller menu that contains it.
units.s: A choice function C for a context (X, D) satisfies condition α if for all A, B ∈ D with A ⊂ B and C(B) ∈ A, we have C(A) = C(B).
units.kw: Sen’s condition α · contraction consistency · Condition alpha (choice functions) · condition α · Condition α · Choice · Rationalizing

units.g: Choice functions induced by preference relations satisfy condition α.
units.s: Let (X, D) be a context and ≿ a preference relation on X such that every A ∈ D has a unique best element under ≿. Then the induced choice function C_≿ satisfies condition α.
units.kw: Sen’s condition α · rational choice · Choice · Rationalizing

units.ti: Rationalizability of choice functions satisfying condition α
units.g: If the domain contains every menu of at most three alternatives, every choice function satisfying condition α is rationalizable.
units.s: Let C be a choice function for a context (X, D) in which D contains every nonempty subset of X with at most three elements. If C satisfies condition α, then C can be rationalized: there is a preference relation ≿ on X with C = C_≿ on D.
units.kw: rationalizability · Sen’s condition α · Choice · Rationalizing

units.g: On a domain closed under unions, condition α suffices for rationalizability.
units.s: Let C be a choice function for a context (X, D) in which A ∪ B ∈ D whenever A, B ∈ D. If C satisfies condition α, then C can be rationalized.
units.kw: rationalizability · revealed preference · Choice · Rationalizing

units.g: A decision maker examines alternatives in a fixed order and takes the first satisfactory one.
units.s: Let (X, D) be a context, v : X → ℝ a valuation, v* ∈ ℝ a threshold, and O an ordering of X (complete, asymmetric and transitive). Assume that every A ∈ D has a unique satisficing choice. The satisficing choice function C_v,v*,O assigns to each A ∈ D the first element, in the order O, of x ∈ A : v(x) ≥ v*, if this set is nonempty; the last element of A in the order O, otherwise.
units.kw: satisficing · bounded rationality · Satisficing choice function · Satisficing procedure · Choice · The Satisficing Procedure

units.g: The satisficing procedure produces choices consistent with condition α.
units.s: Let (X, D) be a context, v a valuation, v* a threshold and O an ordering of X such that every A ∈ D has a unique satisficing choice. Then the satisficing choice function C_v,v*,O satisfies condition α.
units.kw: satisficing · Sen’s condition α · Choice · The Satisficing Procedure

units.g: Satisficing choices can always be explained as maximization of some preference relation.
units.s: Let (X, D) be a context, v a valuation, v* a threshold and O an ordering of X such that every A ∈ D has a unique satisficing choice. Then C_v,v*,O can be rationalized: there is a preference relation ≿ on X such that every A ∈ D has a unique best element under ≿ and C_v,v*,O(A) = C_≿(A) for all A ∈ D.
units.kw: satisficing · rationalizability · Satisficing is rationalizable · Simon’s satisficing · Choice · The Satisficing Procedure

units.g: A choice correspondence selects a nonempty set of acceptable alternatives from every menu.
units.s: Given a context (X, D), a choice correspondence C assigns to every A ∈ D a set C(A) with ∅ ≠ C(A) ⊆ A.
units.kw: choice correspondence · Choice correspondence · Choice · Choice Correspondences

units.g: The set of best elements of each menu according to a fixed preference relation.
units.s: Let (X, D) be a context and ≿ a preference relation on X such that every A ∈ D has at least one best element under ≿. The induced choice correspondence is C_≿(A) = x ∈ A : x ≿ y ∀ y ∈ A.
units.kw: rational choice · choice correspondence · Choice correspondence induced by a preference · induced choice correspondence · Choice · Choice Correspondences

units.ti: Weak axiom of revealed preference (choice correspondences)
units.g: Once x is revealed at least as good as y, y is never revealed strictly better than x.
units.s: A choice correspondence C for a context (X, D) satisfies the weak axiom (WA) if for all A, B ∈ D and all x, y ∈ A ∩ B: if x ∈ C(A) and y ∈ C(B), then x ∈ C(B).
units.kw: weak axiom of revealed preference · WARP · Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (choice correspondences) · Weak axiom of revealed preference (WARP) · Choice · Choice Correspondences

units.g: An alternative chosen from a menu remains chosen from any smaller menu that contains it.
units.s: A choice correspondence C for a context (X, D) satisfies condition α if for all A, B ∈ D with A ⊂ B and every a ∈ A: if a ∈ C(B), then a ∈ C(A).
units.kw: Sen’s condition α · Condition alpha (choice correspondences) · condition α (correspondences) · Choice · Choice Correspondences

units.g: Alternatives tied at the top of a menu remain tied when the menu expands.
units.s: A choice correspondence C for a context (X, D) satisfies condition β if for all A, B ∈ D with A ⊂ B and all a, b ∈ A: if a, b ∈ C(A) and b ∈ C(B), then a ∈ C(B).
units.kw: Sen’s condition β · Condition beta (choice correspondences) · condition β · Condition β · Choice · Choice Correspondences

units.ti: Rationalizable choice correspondences (conditions α and β)
units.g: If the domain contains every menu of at most three alternatives, a choice correspondence satisfying α and β is the set of best elements of a preference relation.
units.s: Let C be a choice correspondence for a context (X, D) in which D contains every nonempty subset of X with at most three elements. If C satisfies conditions α and β, then there is a preference relation ≿ on X such that C_≿(A) is nonempty and C(A) = C_≿(A) for every A ∈ D.
units.kw: rationalizability · Sen’s conditions α and β · revealed preference · Rationalizable choice correspondence · Rationalizability by α and β · Choice · Choice Correspondences

units.ti: Conditions α and β versus the weak axiom
units.g: On an intersection-closed domain, conditions α and β together are equivalent to the weak axiom.
units.s: Let C be a choice correspondence for a context (X, D) in which A ∩ B ∈ D whenever A, B ∈ D and A ∩ B ≠ ∅. Then C satisfies conditions α and β if and only if C satisfies WA.
units.kw: WARP · Sen’s conditions α and β · The weak axiom (WARP) · Weak axiom of revealed preference (WARP) · Choice · Choice Correspondences

units.g: Choice problems in which one available alternative is the default.
units.s: An extended choice function on X assigns to every pair (A, a) with A ⊆ X and a ∈ A an element c(A, a) ∈ A. Read c(A, a) = b as: facing the set A with default a, the decision maker chooses b.
units.kw: default option · status quo · Extended choice function (choice with a default) · extended choice function · Choice · Modeling Choice Procedures

units.g: Maximize utility, but give the default a non-negative bonus.
units.s: Let u : X → ℝ be a utility function and β : X → ℝ a bias function with β(x) ≥ 0 for all x, and assume that the procedure below selects exactly one alternative for every pair (A, a). The default-bias procedure DBP_u,β chooses from (A, a) the alternative x ∈ A ∖ a that uniquely maximizes u on A ∖ a, if u(x) > u(a) + β(a); the default a, if u(a) + β(a) ≥ u(x) for every x ∈ A ∖ a.
units.kw: default bias · status quo bias · Default-bias procedure · default-bias procedure · Choice · Modeling Choice Procedures

units.ti: Weak axiom for choice with defaults
units.g: A revealed-preference consistency condition adapted to choice problems with a default.
units.s: An extended choice function c satisfies the weak axiom (WA) if for all sets A, B and all distinct a, b ∈ A ∩ B: it is not the case that c(A, a) = a and c(B, a) = b; for all defaults x ∈ A and y ∈ B outside a, b (not necessarily distinct), it is not the case that c(A, x) = a and c(B, y) = b.
units.kw: weak axiom of revealed preference · default bias · Weak Axiom for choice with a default · weak axiom (choice with defaults) · Choice · Modeling Choice Procedures

units.g: Promoting the chosen alternative to default does not change the choice.
units.s: An extended choice function c satisfies default tendency (DT) if for every set A and every default x ∈ A: if c(A, x) = a, then c(A, a) = a.
units.kw: default tendency · status quo bias · Default Tendency · Choice · Modeling Choice Procedures

units.g: On a finite set, the weak axiom and default tendency characterize choice that maximizes utility with a bonus for the default.
units.s: Let X be finite and let c be an extended choice function on X. Then c satisfies WA and default tendency if and only if c = DBP_u,β for some utility u : X → ℝ and some bias β : X → ℝ with β ≥ 0 for which the procedure is well defined.
units.kw: default bias · status quo bias · revealed preference · Choice · Modeling Choice Procedures

units.g: More of every good is at least as good; strictly more of every good is strictly better.
units.s: A preference relation ≿ on the commodity space X = ℝ^K_+ is monotone if for all bundles x, y ∈ X: if xₖ ≥ yₖ for every k, then x ≿ y; if xₖ > yₖ for every k, then x ≻ y.
units.kw: monotonicity · Monotonicity · monotone preferences · Consumer Preferences

units.g: Any increase in any good, keeping the others, is strictly better.
units.s: A preference relation ≿ on X = ℝ^K_+ is strongly monotone if for all bundles x, y ∈ X: if xₖ ≥ yₖ for every k and x ≠ y, then x ≻ y.
units.kw: strong monotonicity · Strong monotonicity · strongly monotone preferences · Consumer Preferences · Monotonicity

units.g: Arbitrarily close to a bundle there is a strictly better one.
units.s: A preference relation ≿ on X = ℝ^K_+ is nonsatiated at the bundle y if for every ε > 0 there is x ∈ X with d(x, y) < ε and x ≻ y, where d(x,y) = √(Σₖ (xₖ - yₖ)²) is the Euclidean distance.
units.kw: nonsatiation · local nonsatiation · Nonsatiation at a bundle · Consumer Preferences · Monotonicity

units.g: Strict preferences between bundles survive small changes in either bundle.
units.s: A preference relation ≿ on X = ℝ^K_+ is continuous if for all a, b ∈ X with a ≻ b there is ε > 0 such that x ≻ y for all x, y ∈ X with d(x,a) < ε and d(y,b) < ε, where d is the Euclidean distance.
units.kw: continuous preferences · Continuity on the commodity space (single radius) · Consumer Preferences · Continuity

units.ti: Utility representation of monotone continuous preferences
units.g: Monotone and continuous preferences over bundles have a continuous utility representation.
units.s: Let ≿ be a preference relation on X = ℝ^K_+ that is monotone and continuous. Then there is a continuous function u : X → ℝ that represents ≿.
units.kw: utility representation · continuous utility · Consumer Preferences · Existence of a Utility Representation

units.g: Moving toward a weakly better bundle never makes things worse.
units.s: A preference relation ≿ on X = ℝ^K_+ satisfies convexity 1 if for all bundles x, y and all α ∈ (0,1): x ≿ y implies α x + (1-α) y ≿ y.
units.kw: convex preferences · Convexity (Convexity 1) · Consumer Preferences · Convexity

units.g: A mixture of two bundles is at least as good as one of them.
units.s: A preference relation ≿ on X = ℝ^K_+ satisfies convexity 2 if for all bundles x, y, z such that z = α x + (1-α) y for some α ∈ (0,1): z ≿ x or z ≿ y.
units.kw: convex preferences · Convexity 2 (a mixture is at least as good as one endpoint) · Consumer Preferences · Convexity

units.g: Upper contour sets are convex.
units.s: A preference relation ≿ on X = ℝ^K_+ satisfies convexity 3 if for every y ∈ X the upper contour set z ∈ X : z ≿ y is convex: for all bundles a, b and all α ∈ (0,1), a ≿ y and b ≿ y imply α a + (1-α) b ≿ y.
units.kw: convex preferences · upper contour set · Convexity 3 (convex upper contour sets) · Consumer Preferences · Convexity

units.ti: Equivalence of the three definitions of convexity
units.g: The three definitions of convex preferences coincide for every preference relation.
units.s: Let ≿ be a preference relation on X = ℝ^K_+. Then ≿ satisfies convexity 1 if and only if it satisfies convexity 2, if and only if it satisfies convexity 3.
units.kw: convex preferences · Consumer Preferences

units.g: Strict mixtures of distinct bundles that are at least as good as y are strictly better than y.
units.s: A preference relation ≿ on X = ℝ^K_+ is strictly convex if for all bundles a, b, y with a ≠ b and all λ ∈ (0,1): a ≿ y and b ≿ y imply λ a + (1-λ) b ≻ y.
units.kw: strictly convex preferences · Strict convexity · Consumer Preferences · Convexity

units.g: A reminder of the mathematical definitions used in the link between convexity and utility.
units.s: A function u is concave if u(λ x + (1-λ) y) ≥ λ u(x) + (1-λ) u(y) for all x, y and λ ∈ [0,1], and quasi-concave if for every y the set x : u(x) ≥ u(y) is convex. Every concave function is quasi-concave.
units.kw: quasi-concave function · concave function · Consumer Preferences

units.g: A represented preference is convex exactly when its utility function is quasi-concave.
units.s: Let ≿ be a preference relation on X = ℝ^K_+ and let u : X → ℝ represent ≿. Then ≿ is convex if and only if u is quasi-concave, that is, for every y ∈ X the set x ∈ X : u(x) ≥ u(y) is convex.
units.kw: quasi-concave utility · convex preferences · Quasi-concave utility function · Convexity and quasi-concavity · Quasi-concave utility · Consumer Preferences

units.ti: Convex preferences need not have a concave utility
units.g: Some continuous and convex preference on ℝ is represented by no concave function.
units.s: There exists a preference relation ≿ on X = ℝ that is continuous and convex but is represented by no concave utility function. One such relation is x ≿ y ⟺ x ≥ y or y ≤ 0. Change from the printed example: y ≤ 0 replaces y < 0; nothing else differs.
units.kw: concave utility · convex preferences · Continuity of a preference on the real line · Convexity of a preference on the real line · Concave utility representation · As printed: a continuous convex preference with no concave utility · The printed example relation is not continuous · Consumer Preferences

units.g: Convexity as the existence, at every alternative, of a criterion that must improve.
units.s: Let Λ be a set of orderings (criteria) on X, each criterion with strict part . A preference relation ≿ on X is Λ-convex if for every y ∈ X there is ∈ Λ with x : x ≻ y ⊆ x : x y. Such a criterion is a critical ordering at y; it need not be unique.
units.kw: Λ-convexity · critical ordering · Lambda-convexity (book definition) · Consumer Preferences · Another Perspective on the Convexity of Preferences

units.g: The strict version of Λ-convexity, covering moves to equally good alternatives.
units.s: With Λ as above, a preference relation ≿ on X is Λ-strictly convex if for every y ∈ X there is ∈ Λ with x : x ≿ y, x ≠ y ⊆ x : x y.
units.kw: Λ-convexity · Lambda-strict convexity · Λ-strict convexity · Consumer Preferences · Another Perspective on the Convexity of Preferences

units.ti: Λ-convexity on finite sets: the bottom-up construction
units.g: On a finite set, Λ-convex preferences are exactly those built by placing Λ-minimal alternatives one at a time.
units.s: Let X be finite and Λ a set of strict orderings on X. A preference relation ≿ on X is Λ-convex if and only if it can be constructed from the bottom up as follows: at each step, choose an alternative that is minimal, according to one of the orderings in Λ, among the alternatives not yet ranked, and place it weakly or strictly above those already ranked.
units.kw: Λ-convexity · Constructible by the bottom-up placement procedure · Consumer Preferences

units.g: Preferences on an interval with a unique ideal point, declining on both sides.
units.s: A preference relation ≿ on X = [0,1] is single-peaked if there is a point p, the peak, such that p ≿ x for all x, and p is the only point with this property; ≿ is strictly increasing below the peak: a < b ≤ p implies b ≻ a; ≿ is strictly decreasing above the peak: p ≤ a < b implies a ≻ b.
units.kw: single-peaked preferences · Single-peaked preference on [0, 1] · Single-peaked preferences · Consumer Preferences · Single-Peak Orderings

units.ti: Single-peaked preferences as Λ-strictly convex preferences
units.g: On [0, 1], continuous single-peaked preferences are the Λ-strictly convex ones for the left and right criteria.
units.s: Let ≿ be a continuous preference relation on X = [0,1] and let Λ = _L, _R, where _R ranks points farther to the right higher (x _R y iff x > y) and _L ranks points farther to the left higher (x _L y iff x < y). Then ≿ is Λ-strictly convex if and only if it is single-peaked.
units.kw: single-peaked preferences · Λ-convexity · Continuity of a preference on [0, 1] · Consumer Preferences · Single-Peak Orderings

units.g: Orderings of bundles by a fixed linear value vector.
units.s: For a vector v ∈ ℝ^K with v ≠ 0, the algebraic linear ordering ≥v on bundles in X = ℝ^K+ is defined by x ≥_v y iff v · x ≥ v · y; its strict part is x >_v y iff v · x > v · y. Let Ψ be the set of all algebraic linear orderings.
units.kw: algebraic linear ordering · Psi-convexity (algebraic linear orderings) · Consumer Preferences · Euclidean Space with Algebraic Linear Orderings

units.g: Ψ-convexity, the separating-hyperplane form of convexity, implies convexity; the converse needs interior bundles.
units.s: Let there be at least one good (K ≥ 1) and let ≿ be a continuous, convex preference relation on X = ℝ^K_+. topics.title: Preferences
topics.blurb: Preference relations are the primitive of choice theory: complete and transitive rankings, from which strict preference and indifference are derived. The two classical definitions, by questionnaire and by relation, describe the same objects.

topics.title: Utility representation
topics.blurb: A utility function represents a preference when higher numbers mean better alternatives. Preferences on countable sets always have one, continuous preferences on connected subsets of Euclidean space have a continuous one (Debreu), and the lexicographic preference on the square has none.

topics.title: Choice and rationalizability
topics.blurb: Choice functions record what a decision maker picks from each set of alternatives. The central question is rationalizability, whether the choices maximize some preference; conditions α and β and the weak axiom of revealed preference answer it.

topics.title: Consumer preferences
topics.blurb: Preferences over bundles carry economic structure: monotonicity, continuity, convexity, homotheticity, quasi-linearity and differentiability. Each has a counterpart in utility, such as quasi-concavity for convexity and homogeneity for homotheticity.

topics.title: Consumer demand and duality
topics.blurb: The consumer chooses a best bundle in the budget set, and demand records that choice at every price and wealth. The entries run from Walras’ law and first-order conditions to Roy’s identity and the duality with expenditure minimization.

topics.title: Producers and the firm
topics.blurb: A producer is described by a technology, the set of feasible plans, or by a production function. Profit maximization gives the profit and supply functions, with Hotelling’s lemma, and cost minimization gives the cost function.

topics.title: Choice under uncertainty
topics.blurb: Choice under uncertainty ranks lotteries over prizes. Preferences satisfying independence and continuity have an expected-utility representation (von Neumann–Morgenstern), and de Finetti’s theorem derives subjective probabilities from preferences over bets.

topics.title: Risk attitudes
topics.blurb: For monetary lotteries, attitudes toward risk are read off the vNM utility. On an interval of prizes, risk aversion is concavity and being more risk averse is a concave transformation; first-order stochastic dominance is the ranking that every expected-utility maximizer who prefers more money shares.

topics.title: Social choice
topics.blurb: Social choice aggregates individual preferences into a social ranking or decision. With at least three alternatives, Arrow’s theorem leaves only dictatorships under Pareto and independence of irrelevant alternatives; related entries treat strategy-proofness, majority rule and single-peaked preferences.

topics.title: Games and equilibrium
topics.blurb: Strategic games, best responses and equilibrium.

topics.title: Behavioral decision theory
topics.blurb: Some choice procedures depart from maximizing a single preference, or reach consistent choices by other routes. Examples include Simon’s satisficing, choice with a default and a bias toward it, choice from lists and Luce’s probabilistic choice.

topics.title: Contracts and incentives
topics.blurb: Moral hazard and the design of incentive contracts.
